newsitem.title: USA: Tennessee public hospital to appeal ruling.
newsitem.headline: Tennessee public hospital to appeal ruling.

text.p: A public hospital in Madison County, Tenn., will appeal a court ruling that barred its interest in an eyecare network that opponents claimed was anti-competitive, a hospital attorney said Monday.
The Madison County Chancery Court ruled in June that the not-for-profit Jackson-Madison County General Hospital had no legal authority to set up its Sight Care Network.
Chancellor Joe Morris sided with five opthalmologists who had sought to join the network but were told their services were unneeded.
They sued, claiming that by excluding them from the network, the hospital had granted an illegal franchise to competing ophthalmologists with whom it contracted to treat patients in the network.
In ruling against the hospital, Morris threw into question a measure passed by the legislature last year.

The legislation gave city- and county-owned hospitals that were created by private acts of the legislature greater authorty to form provider networks and partnerships. The Madison hospital was created by a private act.

The hospital has filed legal notice of its intent to appeal the ruling to the state Court of Appeals. If the appeal fails, the fight could go to the Tennessee Supreme Court, Mandy Young, one of the hospital's attorneys, said Monday.
The Tennessee Attorney General's Office is also involved in the case, defending the constitutionality of the 1996 statute.

Hospital administrators told the plaintiffs they could apply to participate in the hospital eyecare network only if an ophthalmic surgery center developed by the plaintiffs was closed down, the suit said.

"The actual reason for the exclusion of Eye Clinic physicians from memberships in the Sight Care Network is purely anti-competitive," the lawsuit said. "This exclusionary action was taken by the (hospital) District to punish and discipline the plaintiffs for setting up an ambulatory surgery treatment center which competes with the District's West Tennessee Surgery Center."
The lawsuit contends it is unconstitutional for the public hospital to participate in a joint ownership venture with a private enterprise.
The hospital countered that since it was created by a private legislative act it is not a municipal entity and should not have to operate according to rules that govern those entities.
